kp: Anthropic certification tracks and exam logistics
subject: eecs
stem: An architect is scheduling the CCAR-F exam and wants to confirm its format before booking. Which description is correct?
options: 60 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, scaled 100–1000, passing at 720
100 questions in 90 minutes, scored as a simple percentage, passing at 70%
40 open-book questions in 60 minutes with no fixed cutoff
A live oral interview with an Anthropic engineer, graded pass or fail
explain: CCAR-F is 60 multiple-choice items in 120 minutes, scaled 100–1000 with 720 to pass. The distractors invent a percentage grade, an open-book format, and an interview — none match the published logistics.

kp: Anthropic certification tracks and exam logistics
subject: eecs
stem: A candidate finishes CCAR-F with a scaled score of 715. What is the outcome?
options: Fail — 720 is the passing score and 715 is below it
Pass — anything above 700 clears CCAR-F
Pass — the cutoff is a percentage and 715 of 1000 is over 70%
A provisional pass pending manual review
explain: The scale runs 100–1000 and the cutoff is 720, so 715 fails. There is no 700 threshold, the cutoff is a scaled score not a percentage, and there is no provisional-review path.

kp: Anthropic certification tracks and exam logistics
subject: eecs
stem: An architect has limited study time and wants to prioritize by exam weight. Which domain carries the MOST questions on CCAR-F?
options: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration (27%)
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output (20%)
Tool Design & MCP Integration (18%)
Context Management & Reliability (15%)
explain: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration is weighted 27%, the heaviest of the five domains. Prompt Engineering (20%), Tool Design & MCP (18%), and Context & Reliability (15%) each carry fewer questions.

kp: The agent loop: model, tools, environment
subject: eecs
stem: While driving the Messages API, an architect receives a response whose stop_reason is tool_use. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Execute the requested tool, append its result, and call the API again
Return the model's text to the user as the final answer
Treat it as an error and restart the conversation
Raise max_tokens and resend the identical request
explain: A stop_reason of tool_use means the model is requesting a tool; you run it, append the tool_result, and continue the loop. It is not the final turn (that is end_turn), not an error, and not a token-limit issue (that is max_tokens).

kp: The agent loop: model, tools, environment
subject: eecs
stem: A response comes back with stop_reason of end_turn and no tool call. What does this indicate?
options: The model finished its turn naturally; the loop can stop
The model was cut off by the token limit
A tool must be run before continuing
A stop sequence was hit in the middle of a tool call
explain: end_turn means the model completed its turn, so the loop ends. max_tokens signals truncation, tool_use signals a pending tool call, and stop_sequence means a configured stop string was emitted.

kp: The agent loop: model, tools, environment
subject: eecs
stem: A developer calls the raw Messages API and expects tool calls to run automatically, but their tools never execute. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: With the Messages API the loop lives in your code; you must detect tool_use and run the tool yourself
The API only runs tools when temperature is set to 0
Tool execution requires the Batch API
Tools run only if you omit the system prompt
explain: The Messages API does not execute tools; your code must detect tool_use, run the tool, and re-call the API. Temperature, the Batch API, and the system prompt have nothing to do with who runs the loop.

kp: The agent loop: model, tools, environment
subject: eecs
stem: In the agent loop, what role do tool results play?
options: They are the environment feedback the model reads to decide its next action
They are discarded once logged and never seen by the model
They replace the system prompt on the next turn
They are used only to compute a final score
explain: Tool results are appended as the environment's feedback, letting the model observe the outcome and plan the next step. They are not discarded, do not overwrite the system prompt, and are not a scoring device.

kp: Orchestration patterns: single agent, subagents, pipelines
subject: eecs
stem: An architect must process 500 independent documents, each summarized the same way, as fast as possible. Which orchestration approach is MOST appropriate?
options: A fan-out pipeline of parallel workers, since the tasks are independent
A single agent looping over all 500 documents in one context window
One subagent that reads all 500 into its window and returns a report
A chain where each document's summary is fed into the next
explain: Independent, parallelizable work fits a fan-out orchestrator-worker pipeline. A single looping agent is slow and context-heavy, cramming all 500 into one window overflows it, and chaining wrongly serializes independent tasks.

kp: Orchestration patterns: single agent, subagents, pipelines
subject: eecs
stem: A task needs an agent to read a very large log file and act on just a few findings, without polluting the main conversation. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Delegate to a subagent that reads the log in its own window and returns a summary
Paste the entire log into the main agent's context
Split the work across many parallel workers that each receive the full log
Force JSON output from the main agent
explain: A subagent isolates the bulky read in a fresh window and returns only a summary, protecting the main context. Pasting the full log bloats context, giving every worker the full log wastes tokens, and forcing JSON does not address context size.

kp: Orchestration patterns: single agent, subagents, pipelines
subject: eecs
stem: A team's first instinct for a new feature is a five-agent system. What does the guidance recommend they try FIRST?
options: A single agent with well-designed tools
A five-agent orchestrator-worker mesh
One agent per data source, always
A pipeline regardless of whether the work is parallel
explain: Start with a single agent with good tools; it has fewer moving parts and is easier to debug. Multi-agent meshes, per-source agents, and forced pipelines add coordination cost and are justified only by real context or parallelism needs.

kp: Orchestration patterns: single agent, subagents, pipelines
subject: eecs
stem: What is the defining benefit of using a subagent?
options: It isolates context, running in a fresh window and returning only a summary
It guarantees lower latency than a single agent in every case
It removes the need for tool allowlists
It shares the parent's full context window by reference
explain: A subagent's value is context isolation — a fresh window, a scoped task, a summary back. It does not always cut latency, does not replace allowlists, and specifically does not share the parent's full window.

kp: Guardrails and autonomy: approvals, allowlists, stop conditions
subject: eecs
stem: An architect is deciding which agent actions may run without approval. According to the guiding principle, autonomy should scale with what?
options: Reversibility — the easier an action is to undo, the more it can be automated
The model's confidence score on that action
The number of tools available to the agent
The size of the context window
explain: The principle is that autonomy scales with reversibility: auto-run easily undone actions, gate irreversible ones. Confidence scores, tool count, and window size do not determine how safe automation is.

kp: Guardrails and autonomy: approvals, allowlists, stop conditions
subject: eecs
stem: An agent can call a read-only list_orders tool and a destructive delete_order tool. What is the MOST appropriate permission design?
options: Auto-run list_orders; require approval for delete_order
Auto-run both so the agent stays fast
Require approval for both, including the read
Deny both and disable the agent
explain: Tier by risk: read-only actions can run automatically, mutating or destructive ones require approval. Auto-running the delete is unsafe, gating a harmless read is needless friction, and denying both defeats the purpose.

kp: Guardrails and autonomy: approvals, allowlists, stop conditions
subject: eecs
stem: A team wants to ensure an agent can never call a payment API, no matter what the model decides. What is the MOST reliable control?
options: A tool allowlist that simply does not include the payment tool
A sentence in the prompt asking the model not to use it
A higher temperature to reduce risky calls
Trusting the model to restrain itself
explain: An allowlist constrains what can be called at all — if the payment tool is not on it, it cannot be invoked. A prompt request, temperature, and self-restraint are all non-deterministic and can be overridden by the model.

kp: Guardrails and autonomy: approvals, allowlists, stop conditions
subject: eecs
stem: An autonomous agent occasionally loops indefinitely, burning budget. Which control MOST directly prevents this?
options: Max-iteration limits and budget stops
A longer system prompt
Forcing JSON output
Switching transports from stdio to HTTP
explain: Max-iteration caps and budget stops bound runaway loops directly. A longer prompt, forced JSON, and transport choice do nothing to halt an agent that keeps iterating.

kp: Claude Agent SDK core abstractions
subject: eecs
stem: An architect wants the agent loop, permission modes, hooks, and MCP connections handled for them rather than hand-built. Which is the MOST appropriate choice?
options: The Claude Agent SDK, which packages the loop plus that tooling
The raw Messages API, implementing the loop themselves
The Batch API for asynchronous jobs
A single forced tool call
explain: The Agent SDK bundles the loop, permission modes, hooks, and MCP so you do not build them yourself. The Messages API makes you own the loop, the Batch API is for bulk async work, and a forced tool call is a single-call technique, not an agent runtime.

kp: Claude Agent SDK core abstractions
subject: eecs
stem: A developer chose the raw Messages API and is surprised they must write the tool-execution loop by hand. Which statement explains this correctly?
options: The Messages API leaves the loop to you; the Agent SDK is what provides it
The Messages API runs the loop but only for MCP tools
Neither the Messages API nor the Agent SDK ever runs the loop
The Agent SDK removes the ability to define custom tools
explain: With the Messages API you own the loop; the Agent SDK supplies it. The Messages API does not run any loop, the SDK does run it, and the SDK still supports custom tool definitions.

kp: Claude Agent SDK core abstractions
subject: eecs
stem: Which set of capabilities does the Claude Agent SDK package into one runtime?
options: The agent loop, tool definitions, hooks, permission modes, MCP connections, and session management
Only a chat UI with no tool support
A database and a vector store
A billing dashboard and usage alerts
explain: The SDK packages the loop (query and client), tools, hooks, permission modes, MCP connections, and session management. It is not a UI, a datastore, or a billing product.

kp: Claude Agent SDK core abstractions
subject: eecs
stem: Why do agents built on the Claude Agent SDK inherit Claude Code's permission model and hooks?
options: The SDK is built on the same harness that powers Claude Code
The SDK copies Claude Code's source into each project
The Claude Code CLI must be installed at runtime
The permission model is re-implemented differently in the SDK
explain: The SDK shares the harness underlying Claude Code, so it inherits the same permission model, hooks, and MCP integration. It does not copy source per project, does not require the CLI at runtime, and does not diverge in its permission model.

kp: Tool schema design: descriptions, parameters, misuse resistance
subject: eecs
stem: An agent frequently calls the wrong tool among several similar ones. Which improvement to the tool descriptions will help MOST?
options: State WHEN to use each tool, not just what it does
Make every description as short as possible
Give all of them the same generic description
Remove the descriptions and rely on the tool names
explain: Descriptions that say WHEN to reach for a tool disambiguate similar tools. Overly short, identical, or missing descriptions remove exactly the usage cues the model needs to choose correctly.

kp: Tool schema design: descriptions, parameters, misuse resistance
subject: eecs
stem: A get_user tool has the description get a user, and the model keeps calling it needlessly. What is the BEST fix?
options: Describe WHEN to call it — for example, only when you need a user's email or role by id
Rename it to fetch_user while keeping the same description
Raise the difficulty of the surrounding questions
Force the model to always call it first
explain: Adding WHEN-to-use guidance stops needless calls. Renaming keeps the same ambiguity, difficulty is unrelated, and forcing the call makes the overuse worse.

kp: Tool schema design: descriptions, parameters, misuse resistance
subject: eecs
stem: A toolset has five overlapping search tools and the model hesitates or picks inconsistently. What is the MOST appropriate redesign?
options: Consolidate into a few orthogonal tools with clear, non-overlapping purposes
Add a sixth search tool to cover the gaps
Give all five the same name
Remove all search capability
explain: Few, orthogonal tools reduce the model's hesitation. Adding more overlap worsens it, identical names create ambiguity, and removing search throws out needed capability.

kp: Tool schema design: descriptions, parameters, misuse resistance
subject: eecs
stem: When a tool call fails on bad input, which return value BEST helps the model recover on its own?
options: A structured error naming what went wrong and listing the valid options
A generic message that just says failed, with no detail
A silent empty result
A stack trace of the server's internals
explain: An actionable error (what failed, how to fix, valid values) lets the next call self-correct. A generic message, a silent empty result, and an internal stack trace give the model nothing useful to act on.

kp: MCP architecture: hosts, clients, servers, transports
subject: eecs
stem: In MCP, what is the relationship between a client and a server?
options: One client connects to exactly one server (1:1), and the host holds multiple clients
One client multiplexes many servers at once
One server connects out to many clients (1:many)
Client and server are the same process
explain: MCP pairs one client to one server (1:1); the host application aggregates several clients, one per server. A single client does not multiplex servers, servers do not fan out to many clients, and client and server are distinct roles.

kp: MCP architecture: hosts, clients, servers, transports
subject: eecs
stem: An architect connects a locally installed MCP server that runs as a subprocess. Which transport is the MOST appropriate?
options: stdio, the transport for local servers
HTTP-based transport, which is required for all servers
A raw TCP socket defined by MCP
WebRTC, for lower latency
explain: stdio is MCP's transport for local subprocess servers; HTTP-based transport is for remote servers. MCP does not define a raw TCP or WebRTC transport for this case.

kp: MCP architecture: hosts, clients, servers, transports
subject: eecs
stem: What is the central value MCP provides to integrations?
options: A standard protocol, so one server works with any MCP-compatible host
A faster model inference engine
Automatic prompt caching for every request
A replacement for OAuth
explain: MCP standardizes integrations so a connector built once works across hosts. It is not an inference engine, not a caching feature, and not an auth replacement — remote servers still use OAuth.

kp: Integrating external services: auth and error handling
subject: eecs
stem: A team is wiring an agent to a third-party API. Where should the API secret live?
options: Server-side in an environment variable, never in the prompt
In the system prompt so the model can authenticate
In a tool description, for convenience
In each user message that needs the tool
explain: Secrets belong server-side in environment variables; putting them in prompts, tool descriptions, or user messages leaks them into context, transcripts, and logs.

kp: Integrating external services: auth and error handling
subject: eecs
stem: A remote MCP server needs only to read calendar events. Which OAuth scoping is MOST appropriate?
options: A least-privilege read-only calendar scope
Full account access, to avoid future changes
No OAuth, sharing a static admin token instead
Write access, in case it is needed later
explain: Least-privilege scoping limits blast radius if the token leaks. Full access, a shared admin token, and speculative write access all widen the risk unnecessarily.

kp: Integrating external services: auth and error handling
subject: eecs
stem: A downstream API returns HTTP 429. What is the MOST appropriate way for the tool to handle it?
options: Return a structured error the model can read, such as rate_limited with a retry_after value
Throw an unhandled exception that crashes the agent loop
Silently return an empty success
Retry instantly in a tight loop forever
explain: Surfacing a structured rate-limit error lets the agent wait and retry sensibly. Crashing the loop, faking success, and hammering with instant retries all make the failure worse.

kp: Settings hierarchy and permission modes
subject: eecs
stem: A project's .claude/settings.json allows a tool, but an enterprise-managed policy denies it. Which wins?
options: The enterprise-managed policy — it sits at the top of the precedence order
The project settings — closest to the code wins
Whichever file was edited most recently
Neither; the conflict disables the tool for everyone
explain: Precedence is enterprise policy, then CLI flags, then local project, then project, then user, so the enterprise deny wins. Proximity to code, edit recency, and a mutual-cancel rule are not how precedence works.

kp: Settings hierarchy and permission modes
subject: eecs
stem: A developer sets an allow rule in ~/.claude/settings.json (user), but the project's .claude/settings.json denies the same tool. What is the effective behavior?
options: Denied — project settings sit above user settings in precedence
Allowed — user settings always take priority
Allowed — the most specific path wins, and the home directory is most specific
Undefined — the two rules cancel out
explain: Project settings outrank user settings, so the deny applies. User settings do not always win, the home directory is not treated as most specific, and the layers do not cancel.

kp: Settings hierarchy and permission modes
subject: eecs
stem: An architect wants Claude Code to plan a change read-only, without editing files or running mutating commands. Which permission mode fits?
options: plan
acceptEdits
bypassPermissions
default
explain: plan mode is read-only planning. acceptEdits auto-applies edits, bypassPermissions skips prompts entirely, and default merely asks on risky actions rather than staying read-only.

kp: Settings hierarchy and permission modes
subject: eecs
stem: In a settings file, a rule reads deny with the specifier Bash(curl:*). What does this express?
options: A deny rule matched by a tool name plus a specifier pattern
A shell alias that rewrites curl commands
A hook that runs before curl
An allowlist entry that permits curl
explain: Permission rules are allow, ask, or deny, matched by a tool plus an optional specifier like Bash(curl:*); here it denies matching curl calls. It is not an alias, a hook, or an allow entry.

kp: CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks
subject: eecs
stem: A team requires that a linter run after every file edit, with no exceptions. What is the MOST appropriate mechanism?
options: A PostToolUse hook, because it runs deterministically
A line in CLAUDE.md asking the model to lint
A skill the model may load when it seems relevant
A comment in the source files
explain: Hooks fire deterministically on lifecycle events, so a PostToolUse hook guarantees the lint. A CLAUDE.md request or a skill is advisory — the model can skip it — and a source comment does nothing automatically.

kp: CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks
subject: eecs
stem: Which principle BEST captures when to use a hook versus a prompt instruction?
options: Use a hook when it MUST happen, a prompt when it SHOULD
Use a hook for anything a prompt could also do
Use a prompt for security-critical steps
Hooks and prompts are interchangeable
explain: Hooks are for MUST (deterministic), prompts for SHOULD (advisory). Using hooks for everything is overkill, security-critical steps need the determinism of hooks not prompts, and the two are not interchangeable.

kp: CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks
subject: eecs
stem: An architect wants project conventions available in every Claude Code session automatically. Where do they belong?
options: In CLAUDE.md, which loads each session and can import files via @path
In a skill that loads only when the model decides it is relevant
In a PreToolUse hook
In the user's shell profile
explain: CLAUDE.md is persistent per-session project context and supports @path imports. A skill loads on demand not always, a hook runs on tool events not as standing context, and a shell profile is unrelated to Claude Code context.

kp: CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks
subject: eecs
stem: A large body of specialized instructions is only needed occasionally. What is the MOST appropriate way to make it available without bloating every session?
options: Package it as a skill (SKILL.md plus assets) the model loads on demand
Paste all of it into CLAUDE.md
Put it in a Stop hook
Inline it in every user message
explain: A skill is an on-demand instruction pack loaded when relevant, keeping base context lean. CLAUDE.md loads every session (bloat), a Stop hook is a lifecycle command not reference material, and inlining it everywhere wastes context.

kp: Headless mode and CI/CD integration
subject: eecs
stem: An architect wants to run Claude Code inside a CI job, non-interactively. Which invocation is the starting point?
options: claude -p with a prompt (print mode)
claude with no flags, waiting for interactive input
the Batch API
opening the desktop app inside CI
explain: claude -p (print mode) runs non-interactively and is the basis for automation. Interactive mode blocks in CI, the Batch API is an Anthropic API feature not the CLI, and the desktop app cannot run in a pipeline.

kp: Headless mode and CI/CD integration
subject: eecs
stem: A CI job runs claude -p to review pull requests. What is the MOST appropriate risk control?
options: Scope it with --allowedTools to read and comment, not push or deploy
Grant full tool access so it can fix issues automatically
Run it in bypassPermissions with write access to production
Disable exit codes so failures do not stop the pipeline
explain: Scoping tools to read-and-comment prevents an unattended run from causing irreversible damage. Full access, bypass with production write, and hiding failures all remove the guardrails CI most needs.

kp: Headless mode and CI/CD integration
subject: eecs
stem: A pipeline needs to parse Claude Code's output programmatically. Which flag is MOST appropriate?
options: --output-format json (or stream-json)
--verbose
--model
there is no machine-readable output
explain: --output-format json or stream-json yields machine-readable results for pipelines. --verbose and --model do not structure the output, and machine-readable output does exist.

kp: Headless mode and CI/CD integration
subject: eecs
stem: Which is a typical headless Claude Code automation pattern?
options: Automated issue triage or PR review via GitHub Actions
Real-time voice chat with end users
Serving a public web page
Training a new base model
explain: Issue triage, PR review, and scheduled jobs (often via GitHub Actions) are typical headless patterns. Voice chat, web serving, and model training are not what headless Claude Code is for.

kp: System prompts and instruction hierarchy
subject: eecs
stem: An architect is designing a support bot. Where should the role, tone, and output-format rules live?
options: In the system prompt, with only the specific ticket text in the user message
In the user message, rebuilt on every request
Split at random between system and user
In a tool description
explain: Durable role, tone, and format rules belong in the system prompt; the user turn carries the task (the ticket). Rebuilding them per request breaks caching and authority, random splitting is arbitrary, and a tool description is the wrong place.

kp: System prompts and instruction hierarchy
subject: eecs
stem: To make a long, stable instruction block cache-friendly across requests, where should it sit relative to volatile per-request data?
options: Early, before the volatile content, so the prefix stays identical
After the volatile content, at the end of the prompt
Interleaved with the volatile content
Placement does not matter for caching
explain: Prompt caching needs an identical prefix, so stable content goes first and volatile content last. Placing it after or interleaving it changes the prefix each call and misses cache hits; ordering very much matters.

kp: System prompts and instruction hierarchy
subject: eecs
stem: Within a single turn, the system prompt says reply in JSON but the user message says reply in plain prose. How does the instruction hierarchy resolve this?
options: Toward the system prompt — it holds the higher authority
Toward the user message — the latest instruction wins
The request errors out
The model picks one at random each time
explain: Conflicts resolve toward system over user within a turn. It is not last-wins, it does not error, and it is not random — system-level instructions carry higher authority.

kp: System prompts and instruction hierarchy
subject: eecs
stem: An architect wants the model to clearly separate context from the task and return a specific shape. Which technique is recommended?
options: Use XML tags to structure sections and state an explicit output contract
Remove all structure and write one long paragraph
Rely on the model to guess the format
Put everything in ALL CAPS
explain: XML tags plus an explicit output contract make structure and expected shape clear. A single unstructured paragraph, guessing, and all-caps do not reliably convey structure.

kp: Structured output: JSON mode and forced tool use
subject: eecs
stem: An architect needs guaranteed, schema-valid JSON from every call. Which approach is the MOST reliable?
options: Force tool_choice to a specific named tool whose schema defines the output
Ask for JSON in the prompt and parse whatever comes back
Raise max_tokens so the JSON is not truncated
Lower temperature to 0 and hope for valid JSON
explain: Forcing a specific tool makes the model return arguments validated against that tool's JSON Schema — the most reliable structured output. Prose requests, higher token limits, and low temperature reduce but do not remove the risk of malformed output.

kp: Structured output: JSON mode and forced tool use
subject: eecs
stem: A pipeline must extract fields into a fixed schema with zero tolerance for stray prose. What BEST guarantees the shape?
options: Define a tool with that schema and set tool_choice to force it
Append please output only JSON to the user turn
Use a stop sequence of a closing brace
Add few-shot examples until it looks perfect
explain: A forced tool call validates arguments against the schema, so no stray prose leaks. A polite instruction, a brace stop sequence, and more examples all improve the odds but cannot guarantee the shape the way a forced schema does.

kp: Structured output: JSON mode and forced tool use
subject: eecs
stem: For an open-ended brainstorming task that needs free-form reasoning, is forcing a rigid JSON schema advisable?
options: No — rigid structure suppresses the open reasoning you want
Yes — always force a schema for every task
Yes — schemas make brainstorming more creative
It has no effect either way
explain: Forcing a schema on open-ended reasoning constrains the thinking you are after, so it is not advisable there. Forcing schemas is not universally right, does not boost creativity, and does affect the output.

kp: Structured output: JSON mode and forced tool use
subject: eecs
stem: Despite guidance, a small fraction of responses still fail to parse as valid JSON. What is the MOST appropriate production handling?
options: Validate the output and retry on failure, treating it as recoverable
Crash the job on the first parse error
Log the error and silently drop the record
Disable structured output entirely
explain: Validate-then-retry treats a parse failure as recoverable and keeps throughput. Crashing is brittle, silently dropping loses data, and disabling structured output abandons the requirement.

kp: Few-shot, chain-of-thought, and eval-driven iteration
subject: eecs
stem: A model follows the desired output format inconsistently despite a detailed written description. What is the MOST effective next step?
options: Add two or three worked examples of the exact format
Make the written description twice as long
Raise temperature to encourage variety
Switch to a smaller model
explain: For format, examples beat instructions — a few worked examples convey shape better than prose. A longer description, higher temperature (more variety), and a smaller model do not reliably fix format adherence.

kp: Few-shot, chain-of-thought, and eval-driven iteration
subject: eecs
stem: An architect tunes a prompt against a single example until it works perfectly, then sees regressions elsewhere. What went wrong?
options: The prompt overfit to one example instead of the general pattern
The example was too short
The temperature was too low
The model lacked a tool allowlist
explain: Optimizing against one example overfits to that case and regresses on unseen ones; a small eval set of real failures prevents this. Example length, temperature, and allowlists are not the cause.

kp: Few-shot, chain-of-thought, and eval-driven iteration
subject: eecs
stem: A task involves hard, multi-step reasoning. What is the trade-off of enabling chain-of-thought or extended thinking?
options: Better reasoning at the cost of more tokens and latency
Worse reasoning but lower cost
No change in either quality or cost
It affects only formatting, not reasoning
explain: Extended thinking improves hard reasoning but spends more tokens and time, so use it where problems are genuinely hard. It does not worsen reasoning, is not cost-free, and affects reasoning not just formatting.

kp: Few-shot, chain-of-thought, and eval-driven iteration
subject: eecs
stem: What is the recommended way to improve a prompt systematically rather than by guesswork?
options: Build a small eval set from real failures and iterate prompt, then eval, then prompt
Ship each change straight to production and watch for complaints
Judge quality from a single output each time
Never change the prompt once it is written
explain: An eval-driven loop (prompt, then eval, then prompt) measures each change against real failures. Shipping blind, judging by one output, and freezing the prompt all skip measurement.

kp: Context windows and prompt caching
subject: eecs
stem: A team enables prompt caching but sees almost no cache hits. They prepend a per-request timestamp to the prompt. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The changing timestamp alters the prefix, and a cache hit needs an identical prefix
Caching only works with the Batch API
The context window is too large to cache
Cache hits require temperature 0
explain: A cache hit needs a byte-identical prefix; a leading timestamp changes it every call, so nothing hits. Caching is independent of the Batch API, is not blocked by window size, and does not depend on temperature.

kp: Context windows and prompt caching
subject: eecs
stem: To maximize cache hits, how should content be ordered in the prompt?
options: Stable content first, volatile content last
Volatile content first, so it is easy to update
Randomly, since order is irrelevant
Largest content last, regardless of stability
explain: Ordering stable-to-volatile keeps the cached prefix intact for reuse. Putting volatile content first busts the prefix, order is not irrelevant, and sorting by size ignores what actually matters, which is stability.

kp: Context windows and prompt caching
subject: eecs
stem: Which statement about Claude prompt-caching economics is correct?
options: Default TTL is about 5 minutes (refreshing on use); reads cost roughly 0.1x and writes roughly 1.25x of base input
Cache entries last forever once written
Cache reads cost more than cache writes
Caching doubles the cost of every request
explain: The default cache TTL is about 5 minutes, refreshing on use, with reads near 0.1x and writes near 1.25x of base input. Entries expire, reads are cheaper than writes, and caching lowers cost on hits rather than doubling it.

kp: Long conversations: compaction, externalization, retrieval
subject: eecs
stem: A long agent session risks overflowing its window because a subtask must read many large files. What is the MOST appropriate design?
options: Delegate the reading to a subagent that returns a summary, acting as a context firewall
Keep appending every file to the main context
Raise the temperature to compress the input
Disable prompt caching
explain: A subagent firewalls context: it absorbs the bulky reads in its own window and returns a summary. Appending everything overflows the window, temperature does not compress input, and caching is unrelated to window size.

subject: eecs
stem: An agent must track evolving project state across a very long session without carrying it all in context. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
options: Externalize state to files or a database and retrieve only what each step needs
Keep the entire state inline and resend it every turn
Store the state only in the system prompt
Rely on the model to remember it implicitly
explain: Externalizing state and retrieving on demand keeps the window lean. Resending everything bloats context, the system prompt is not a mutable store, and implicit memory is unreliable across a long session.

stem: A production service hits HTTP 429 and 529 responses under load. What is the MOST appropriate retry strategy?
options: Exponential backoff with jitter, honoring the retry-after header
Immediate fixed-interval retries with no delay
Retry once, then give up permanently
Switch every failing call to the Batch API synchronously
explain: Backoff with jitter plus retry-after spreads load and respects server guidance. Instant fixed retries synchronize and worsen limits, one-and-done drops recoverable work, and the Batch API is async bulk, not a synchronous fallback.

A larger context window
Forced tool use
A longer system prompt

The synchronous Messages API, one request per record in real time
Forced tool use on a single call
A streaming endpoint for live updates
